analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal contracts with for-profit prison companies and helps prisoners prepare for release.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with zero cosponsors, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal government to stop paying private companies to run prisons and detention facilities. It gives six years to move all core prison work — housing, guarding, and disciplining of federal prisoners — to government employees, and eight years to end for-profit contracts for halfway houses and similar community confinement facilities. It also requires yearly inspections of jails holding federal Marshals Service prisoners, and requires prisons to give people leaving custody practical help: counseling on expunging their record, job and education programs, and assistance applying for food assistance, Medicaid, Social Security, a driver's license, and voter registration.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in federal prisons and halfway houses — especially the tens of thousands housed in privately operated facilities — would be held in government-run institutions instead of ones run for profit, with annual inspections required for Marshals Service detention. People leaving federal custody would get practical help restarting their lives: counseling on clearing their record, job and education programs, and hands-on help applying for Medicaid, food assistance, Social Security, a driver's license, and voter registration. Taxpayers would also stop paying a profit margin on incarceration, and federal prison workers would gain the jobs that shift in-house.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal prisoners and people reentering society

how_it_helps.text: It requires that all core correctional services in federal prisons — housing, safeguarding, protecting, and disciplining of prisoners — be performed by government employees within six years, and bans for-profit contracts for community confinement facilities within eight years.
It requires annual inspections of every jail holding US Marshals Service prisoners, to check they meet constitutional, federal, and state standards.

It requires prisons to give people before release counseling on expunging their record, job and education programs, and help applying for Medicaid, food assistance, Social Security, a driver's license, and voter registration — and to tell them what fines and restitution they still owe.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit prison companies such as CoreCivic and GEO Group would lose federal contracts worth billions over the phase-out period, and their investors would bear the loss of that revenue. The Justice Department would take on the cost of moving prisoners into government-run or state and local facilities, and of administering the new reentry counseling duties, without any dedicated funding in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and their investors

drawbacks.text: The phase-out is slow: private companies could keep running federal prisons for six years after enactment and community confinement facilities for eight, so under the bill as written the industry would have remained entrenched well into the late 2020s.

Ending private contracts without enough government-run beds could create capacity problems, since private facilities have been used to house overflow from crowded federal prisons; the bill sets no new funding for replacement capacity.

The reentry provisions add new duties for prison officials — counseling on expungement, assistance applying for Medicaid, food assistance, and voter registration — without any dedicated funding to staff that work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest in scope: federal prisoners would move out of for-profit facilities and get structured help reentering society, and taxpayers would stop paying a profit margin on incarceration. The main costs are logistical: the six- to eight-year timeline recognizes that the federal system would need to build or contract government-run capacity to replace tens of thousands of private beds, and the added reentry duties come with no dedicated funding. A reasonable objection is that phasing out private beds faster than the government can add capacity could worsen overcrowding. On balance the bill's costs were manageable and its aims aligned with existing DOJ policy, but it was so narrowly drafted that its biggest weakness was never its design — it was that almost no other member of Congress supported it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: introduced with no cosponsors, sent to the Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023 without ever getting a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the End For-Profit Prisons Act of 2021 on February 22, 2021, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
On April 28, 2021, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — a step that is often the last stop for a bill a committee does not plan to advance.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit prison companies keep their federal contracts, and the committee leadership avoided a fight over phasing them out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit prison companies keep federal contracts

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 22, 2021; no member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: For-profit prison companies
against.role: CoreCivic and GEO Group, the two companies holding most federal private prison contracts
against.what_they_did: Had a financial stake in keeping their Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts, and have historically lobbied and campaigned against restrictions on private prisons.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or a floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member beyond the sponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: For-profit prison companies (e.g. CoreCivic, GEO Group)
industries.note: The bill phases out their federal Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts: prison operations within six years, community confinement within eight, ending a revenue stream paid from the federal budget. For ordinary people, it removes a system where a company earns more by housing people at lower cost per bed, which research has linked to understaffing and poor conditions.

industries.industry: Government-run and state or local correctional facilities
industries.note: The bill keeps halfay-house and jail beds available to state and local government facilities, whose employees would perform the work for-profit companies lose, but it subjects their facilities to new annual inspections and federal standards.
Requiring core correctional work to be done by government employees shifts jobs and hiring from contractors to the federal prison system.
